name: README by its sections
doc:
# Lumen

Lumen is a tiny static site generator that turns a folder of Markdown files into a fast website. It has no plugins and no config by default.

## Before you begin

You need Node 20 or later and a folder with at least one Markdown file. Check your Node version with `node -v` before you start.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install -g lumen
lumen build ./docs
```

## Theming

You can change the colors and fonts with a `lumen.toml` file at the root of your project. Every key is optional; missing keys keep their defaults.

```toml
[theme]
accent = "#3b82f6"
font = "Inter"
```

## Bug fixes

- Fixed a crash when a file name contained spaces (#212)
- Fixed broken links to headings with emoji (#219)
- Updated the Markdown parser to 4.2.1

## When the build fails

If `lumen build` exits with "no pages found", make sure your files end in `.md` and are not ignored by `.gitignore`. Run with `--verbose` to see every file that was skipped.

## See also

- [Markdown guide](https://commonmark.org)
- [Deploying to GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com)

## License

MIT © 2026 Lumen contributors.

name: article
doc:
# Why local-first software matters

Most of the tools we use every day keep our work on someone else's computer. That is convenient until the service changes its terms, raises its prices or simply disappears, and then years of notes, drafts and decisions go with it.

Local-first software turns this around. Your files live on your device first, and syncing or sharing is something you add, not something you depend on. The app keeps working on a plane, in a basement or during an outage, because nothing essential happens far away.

There are trade-offs. Collaboration is harder to build, backups become your responsibility and some features that rely on large servers are out of reach. Still, for writing and thinking tools, owning the files is worth more than most of what a server can offer.
